stories.title: 続報：マンション修繕談合で国交省の有識者会議が初会合 管理組合の発注を支える仕組みへ
stories.summary: 国交省は10月19日、マンション大規模修繕の談合を受けた有識者会議を初開催。管理組合が適切に業者を選べる仕組みを議論し、年度末に対策をまとめます。
body: 国土交通省は10月19日、マンションの大規模修繕工事をめぐる談合を受けて、再発防止に向けた有識者会議の初会合を開きました。10月6日号でお伝えした、公正取引委員会による談合の認定と国交省の検討会設置の続報です。
公取委は9月、東京都と関東6県の大規模修繕工事計171件で談合があったとして、設計コンサルタント2社と施工業者40社の独占禁止法違反（不当な取引制限）を認定していました。会議では、住民でつくる管理組合が工事を発注するときに、適切な事業者を選べる仕組みづくりなどを議論します。年度末に対策を取りまとめる方針です。
会議は冒頭を除いて非公開でした。国交省によると、委員からは、管理組合には業者の選び方や見積金額が妥当かを判断する材料が足りないとの意見が出ました。談合のもとで工事が行われていたと分かったマンションの管理組合から、損害賠償の請求について相談が寄せられていることも紹介されました。
stories.commentary: マンションの大規模修繕は、だいたい12年から15年に1回。足場が組まれ、建物全体が白いシートに包まれる、あの工事です。費用は住民が毎月積み立ててきた修繕積立金から出ます。発注するのは管理組合、つまり住民の代表です。ところが、住民の多くは建築の素人ですよね。見積もりが3社から出てきても、どれが適正なのか判断できない。だから設計コンサルタントに相談するのですが、今回はその相談相手の側まで談合に加わっていたと認定されました。家を売るときに査定を頼んだ不動産屋さんが、実は買い手と裏でつながっていた。そんな構図に近い話なんです。会議で「判断する材料が足りない」という声が出たのは、まさにそこだと思います。業者を選ぶ力を、住民の側にどう持たせるのか。あるいは住民に任せきりにしない仕組みをつくるのか。その線をどこに引くべきなのか、皆さんはどう思いますか。
briefing: 国交省は9月29日、業界団体に再発防止の取り組みを要請し、その際に有識者会議を設ける方針を明らかにしていました。
初会合の冒頭で、国交省の住宅局長は、管理組合の信頼を裏切る談合は許されないと述べました。会議では、大規模修繕工事の実態や、管理組合が持つ知識やノウハウが足りないことも共有されました。
有識者会議は、管理組合が気をつけるべきことや、適切な事業者を確保する方策を検討します。年度末の取りまとめのあと、2027年度以降の対応も含めて検討を続ける見通しです。

hojosen.title: コンサルの役割
hojosen.body: 大規模修繕では、管理組合が設計コンサルタントに建物の調査や工事の仕様づくり、業者選びの手伝いを頼む「設計監理方式」が広く使われています。本来は住民の側に立って工事費をチェックする役割で、そこが談合に関わったことが問題を深くしています。

hojosen.title: 積立金不足の時代
hojosen.body: 資材や人件費の上昇で修繕工事の費用は上がり続けており、修繕積立金が足りないマンションも少なくありません。国交省は長期修繕計画のガイドラインの見直しにも着手しており、修繕のお金と発注の仕組みの両方が問われています。

en.title: Update: Japan's expert panel on condo repair bid-rigging holds first meeting to back owners' associations
en.summary: On Oct 19, Japan's transport ministry held the first meeting of an expert panel set up after bid-rigging on large-scale condominium repairs. It will discuss how to help owners' associations choose contractors and compile measures by the end of the fiscal year.
body: The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT) held the first meeting of an expert panel on Oct 19 to prevent a repeat of bid-rigging on large-scale repair work for condominium buildings. This follows up on our Oct 6 report on the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC) finding of bid-rigging and the ministry's plan to set up a review panel.

In September, the JFTC, Japan's antitrust watchdog, found bid-rigging on a total of 171 large-scale repair projects in Tokyo and six other prefectures in the surrounding Kanto region, and determined that two design consultants and 40 contractors had violated the Antimonopoly Act through unreasonable restraint of trade. The panel will discuss ways to help owners' associations, which are made up of residents, choose appropriate firms when they order repair work. The ministry plans to compile measures by the end of the fiscal year, which in Japan ends in March.

The meeting was closed to the public except for its opening. According to the ministry, panel members said owners' associations lack the information they need to decide how to choose contractors and whether estimates are reasonable. The ministry also noted that associations at condominiums found to have had work done under bid-rigging have been asking for advice about seeking damages.
en.commentary: Large-scale repairs on a condominium building come around roughly once every 12 to 15 years. It's the job where scaffolding goes up and the whole building gets wrapped in white sheeting. The money comes from the repair reserve fund that residents have been paying into every month. And the one placing the order is the owners' association, in other words, representatives of the residents. But most residents aren't construction experts, right? Even if three companies hand in estimates, they can't tell which one is fair. That's why they turn to a design consultant for advice. This time, though, even that adviser was found to have joined in the bid-rigging. Imagine you're selling your home, and the real estate agent you asked for an appraisal turns out to be secretly working with the buyer. It's a setup a lot like that. When panel members said residents lack the information to judge, I think that's exactly the point. How do you give residents the ability to choose contractors? Or do you build a system that doesn't leave it all up to them? Where do you think that line should be drawn?
briefing: On Sept 29, MLIT asked industry groups to take steps to prevent a recurrence, and at the time announced its plan to set up an expert panel.

At the start of the first meeting, the head of MLIT's Housing Bureau said bid-rigging that betrays the trust of owners' associations cannot be tolerated. The meeting also shared information on how large-scale repairs are actually carried out and on owners' associations' lack of knowledge and know-how.

The panel will look at what owners' associations should watch out for and at ways to secure appropriate contractors. After compiling its findings at the end of the fiscal year, it is expected to keep studying the issue, including steps for fiscal 2027 and beyond.

hojosen.title: The consultant's role
hojosen.body: In large-scale repairs, a common approach is the design-and-supervision method, in which an owners' association hires a design consultant to survey the building, draw up the work specifications and help choose a contractor. The consultant is supposed to be on the residents' side, checking construction costs, which is why its involvement in bid-rigging makes the problem so serious.

hojosen.title: Reserve funds running short
hojosen.body: Rising material and labor costs keep pushing up the price of repair work, and many condominiums don't have enough in their repair reserve funds. MLIT has also begun revising its guidelines for long-term repair plans. Both the money for repairs and the way the work is ordered are now being called into question.
